# Workspace README (README.md)

## sindr

[![CI](https://github.com/steffendybvik/sindr-rs/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/steffendybvik/sindr-rs/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/sindr.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/sindr)
[![docs.rs](https://docs.rs/sindr/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/sindr)
[![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue.svg)](#license)

A circuit simulator you embed in Rust: build a circuit as a typed value, solve it natively or in the browser, and get back numbers checked against ngspice.

### Why sindr

- **Typed in, typed out.** A `Circuit` is a Rust value (or JSON), results are structs, and errors are a `SimError` enum you can match on, not text on stderr.
- **Pure Rust, no C.** No `unsafe` in the solver, no libngspice to install, no global state: run as many simulations in parallel threads as you like.
- **Builds for WebAssembly.** `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with every feature on, so the same engine runs in a web app.
- **Answers design questions.** `check_ratings` says whether each part stays inside its absolute maximum ratings, self-heating flags thermal runaway, and `check_specs` turns `.meas`-style measurements into pass/fail with margins.
- **Real parts as primitives.** 31 element types: the usual R, L, C, sources and semiconductors, plus LEDs, zeners, regulators, op-amps, comparators, relays, fuses, switches, potentiometers, thermistors, photoresistors, transformers and batteries.
- **Checked against ngspice.** Every analysis has golden cases solved by both (below).

### Quick start

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr = "0.1.0-alpha.8"
```

How much current does a red LED draw from 5 V through 220 Ω?

```rust
use sindr::{solve_circuit, Circuit, CircuitElement};

fn main() -> Result<(), sindr::SimError> {
    let circuit = Circuit::new("gnd", vec![
        CircuitElement::VoltageSource { id: "V1".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "gnd".into()], voltage: 5.0, waveform: None },
        CircuitElement::Resistor { id: "R1".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "a".into()], resistance: 220.0 },
        CircuitElement::Led { id: "D1".into(), nodes: ["a".into(), "gnd".into()], color: "red".into(), temperature: 300.15 },
    ]);
    let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;
    let led = result.component_results.iter().find(|c| c.id == "D1").unwrap();
    println!("{:.1} mA, {:.1} mW", led.current_through * 1e3, led.power * 1e3);
    Ok(())
}
```

More in [`sindr/examples/`](./sindr/examples): RC transient, BJT amplifier, Bode plot, DC sweep, a SPICE deck.

### Crates

| Crate | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| [`sindr`](./sindr) | The simulator: operating point, transient, AC, DC and temperature sweeps, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.meas`, ratings checks, SPICE front end |
| [`sindr-core`](./sindr-core) | Data model: `Circuit`, elements, waveforms, design hierarchy (blocks, instances) and part data, with no solver |
| [`sindr-devices`](./sindr-devices) | Device physics: diode family, BJT, MOSFET, JFET, IGBT, varactor, thermistor and photoresistor models |

`sindr` depends on `sindr-core`, which depends on `sindr-devices`. The split lets design tools use `Circuit` without the solver, and lets you use the device-physics models with your own solver, without the `nalgebra` linear-algebra stack. `sindr` re-exports `sindr-core`, so most code needs only `sindr`.

### Accuracy

Each analysis is checked against [ngspice](https://ngspice.sourceforge.io/) 47 on golden circuits solved by both: diodes with their `.model` cards and charge, BJTs, MOSFETs, JFETs, LEDs, controlled sources, transformers, subcircuits. The worst deviation of any quantity at any point, per analysis:

<!-- accuracy:start -->
| Analysis | Cases | Worst relative error | Worst other |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating point | 14 | 7e-6 | — |
| DC sweep | 5 | 4e-5 | — |
| Temperature sweep | 1 | 6e-7 | — |
| AC | 8 | 3e-6 | 1e-4° phase |
| Diode charge (AC) | 2 | 2e-4 | — |
| Noise | 3 | 7e-7 | — |
| Transient | 10 | — | 2.6 % of full scale |
<!-- accuracy:end -->

The transient's worst is a switching BJT's collector on a 3 µs edge, where a 0.4 mV base error becomes 2.6 % of the current; its other cases stay under 0.15 %. Every case, and the tolerance its test holds it to, is in [`docs/ACCURACY.md`](./docs/ACCURACY.md); how the cases are built is in [`sindr/tests/golden/README.md`](./sindr/tests/golden/README.md). Both tables come from the test suite (`scripts/accuracy_table.py`).

### Speed

Medians on an Apple M1 Pro, release build, one thread ([details](./sindr/README.md#performance)):

| Circuit | Time |
|---|---:|
| Operating point, 100 diodes and resistors | 0.93 ms |
| Transient, 100-stage RC ladder, 200 steps | 15 ms |
| Half-wave rectifier, five 50 Hz cycles (5 000 steps) | 9 ms |

CI fails a pull request that makes any benchmark more than 25 % slower.

### Compared with

| | sindr | [`thevenin`](https://crates.io/crates/thevenin) | ngspice bindings (`ngspice-sys`, `elektron_ngspice`, …) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | A simulator built to embed, with design checks | A from-scratch rewrite of ngspice in Rust | The C library behind a Rust API |
| Main input | `Circuit` values or JSON; a SPICE3 subset (feature `spice`) | SPICE netlists and its own Cirq language | Netlist text |
| WebAssembly | Yes | Yes | No |
| Needs a C library | No | No | libngspice |
| Ratings, self-heating, pass/fail specs | Yes | No | No |
| Analyses | op, DC, AC, transient, temperature, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.meas` | Those plus pole-zero, AC sensitivity, Fourier and FFT | All of ngspice's |
| Device models | Shockley diode, Ebers–Moll BJT, MOSFET Level 1, JFET, IGBT, op-amp macromodel, and part-level elements (LED, regulator, relay, battery …) | **Far more:** Gummel–Poon and VBIC, MOSFET levels 1–3 and BSIM, MESFETs, transmission lines, XSPICE code models | All of ngspice's |
| SPICE dialect coverage | A practical subset | **Broad**, close to ngspice's | **Full** ngspice |

Pick ngspice, or `thevenin` for the same in Rust, to run existing SPICE decks and vendor model libraries as they are. Pick sindr to put a simulator inside a Rust program or a web app, describe circuits as data, and ask whether the parts survive.

### SPICE netlist input

A SPICE3 netlist parser ships inside `sindr` behind the optional, default-off `spice` feature (it pulls in `winnow` + `miette`, so the baseline build stays lean):

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr = { version = "0.1.0-alpha.8", features = ["spice"] }
```

```rust,ignore
let netlist = sindr::spice::parse_file("amp.cir")?;
let result = sindr::solve_circuit(&netlist.circuit)?;
```

It reads a practical subset of Berkeley SPICE3f5 decks (R, L, C, V, I, D, Q, X, `.subckt`, `.model`, `.tran`, `.dc`, `.ac`, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.op`, `.ic`, `.nodeset`, `.param`, `.include`, `.lib`), keeps `.subckt` hierarchy as blocks and instances (flattened with `.`-separated naming when simulated), and returns a `SourceMap` to recover original instance paths. `to_netlist` writes a `Circuit` back out, `.subckt`s included. See the [`sindr::spice`](https://docs.rs/sindr/latest/sindr/spice/) module docs for the exact supported subset and strictness options.

`sindr::spice::to_netlist` goes the other way: it writes a `Circuit` as a SPICE deck (R, L, C, V, I with waveforms, D and Q with `.model` cards, E/G/F/H, transformers as L–L–K, and exact R/D equivalents for switches, fuses, potentiometers, LEDs and the like) that ngspice runs and `parse_str` reads back. Elements with no SPICE equivalent are an `ExportError`.

A runnable walkthrough (parse → solve → dispatch directives → render a diagnostic) lives in [`sindr/examples/parse_netlist.rs`](./sindr/examples/parse_netlist.rs):

```bash
cargo run --example parse_netlist --features spice
```

### Status

Pre-release alpha (`0.1.0-alpha.8`), [published on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/sindr). API is liable to change.

### Scope & limitations

sindr is an analog circuit simulator. Digital logic, HDL ingestion, MCU simulation, schematic capture, vendor model cards, Monte-Carlo/pole-zero analyses, BSIM-class device models, and coupled thermal networks (beyond one thermal RC per part) are **not** supported today. SPICE netlist import is available as a parser for a practical subset (see above), not full SPICE3 coverage. See [`LIMITATIONS.md`](./LIMITATIONS.md) for the full breakdown of what's out-of-scope versus not-yet-implemented.

To work on sindr itself, see [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](./CONTRIBUTING.md). AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) should also read [`AGENTS.md`](./AGENTS.md) for layout, conventions, and pitfalls.

# Crate `sindr` README (sindr/README.md)

## sindr

MNA (Modified Nodal Analysis) circuit solver. Build a circuit, call `solve_circuit`, get voltages, currents, and power for every component.

Supports: resistive DC, nonlinear DC (Newton-Raphson), transient (Gear-2, trapezoidal or backward Euler), AC analysis, transfer function (`.tf`), DC sensitivity (`.sens`), DC sweep, and temperature sweep. The solver picks the right path automatically based on what components are in the circuit.

Device physics (BJT, MOSFET, diode models) live in the companion crate [`sindr-devices`](../sindr-devices). The data model (`Circuit`, elements, waveforms, blocks, instances, parts) lives in [`sindr-core`](../sindr-core) and is re-exported here.

### Add to your project

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr = "0.1.0-alpha.8"
```

Serde support is on by default. To disable:

```toml
sindr = { version = "0.1.0-alpha.8", default-features = false }
```

To parse SPICE netlists, enable the optional `spice` feature (off by default):

```toml
sindr = { version = "0.1.0-alpha.8", features = ["spice"] }
```

```rust,ignore
let netlist = sindr::spice::parse_file("amp.cir")?;
let result = sindr::solve_circuit(&netlist.circuit)?;
```

It reads a practical subset of Berkeley SPICE3f5 decks (R, L, C, V, I, D, Q, X, `.subckt`, `.model`, `.tran`, `.dc`, `.ac`, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.op`, `.ic`, `.nodeset`, `.param`, `.include`, `.lib`), keeping `.subckt` hierarchy as blocks and instances, which are flattened with `.`-separated naming when simulated. See the `sindr::spice` module docs for the supported subset and strictness options, or run the worked example:

```bash
cargo run --example parse_netlist --features spice
```

`sindr::spice::to_netlist` goes the other way: it writes a `Circuit` as a SPICE deck (R, L, C, V, I with waveforms, D and Q with `.model` cards, E/G/F/H, transformers as L–L–K, and exact R/D equivalents for switches, fuses, potentiometers, LEDs and the like) that ngspice runs and `parse_str` reads back. Elements with no SPICE equivalent are an `ExportError`.

### Quick start

```rust
use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement, solve_circuit};

let circuit = Circuit {
    ground_node: "gnd".into(),
    components: vec![
        CircuitElement::VoltageSource {
            id: "V1".into(),
            nodes: ["n1".into(), "gnd".into()],
            voltage: 10.0,
            waveform: None,
        },
        CircuitElement::Resistor {
            id: "R1".into(),
            nodes: ["n1".into(), "n2".into()],
            resistance: 1_000.0,
        },
        CircuitElement::Resistor {
            id: "R2".into(),
            nodes: ["n2".into(), "gnd".into()],
            resistance: 2_000.0,
        },
    ],
    ..Default::default()
};

let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;

println!("n2 = {:.3} V", result.node_voltages["n2"]);  // 6.667 V
println!("R1 current = {:.3} mA", result.component_results
    .iter().find(|c| c.id == "R1").unwrap().current_through * 1000.0);
```

### Building circuits

Every component has an `id` (arbitrary string) and `nodes` (node names as strings). One node must match `ground_node` — it is held at 0 V.

#### Passive components

```rust
CircuitElement::Resistor   { id, nodes: [String; 2], resistance: f64 }
CircuitElement::Capacitor  { id, nodes: [String; 2], capacitance: f64 }
CircuitElement::Inductor   { id, nodes: [String; 2], inductance: f64, saturation: Option<InductorSaturation> }
```

Capacitors and inductors trigger transient analysis automatically. In pure DC (no reactive elements, no waveforms), they are treated as open circuits.

An inductor with `saturation: Some(InductorSaturation { i_sat, l_sat })` has a core that saturates: its flux is `λ(i) = l_sat·i + (inductance − l_sat)·i_sat·tanh(i/i_sat)`, so its inductance falls from `inductance` at zero current towards `l_sat` past `i_sat` (to 42 % of the way at `i_sat`, 7 % at `2·i_sat`). A datasheet's saturation current, where L has dropped 20–30 %, is about `0.6·i_sat`. The transient integrates the flux, and AC and noise use the incremental inductance `dλ/di` at the DC current. There's no hysteresis or core loss; add a resistor for loss.

```rust
use sindr_devices::inductor::InductorSaturation;

// 10 µH that saturates around 3 A, keeping 1 µH when saturated.
let l1 = CircuitElement::Inductor {
    id: "L1".into(),
    nodes: ["sw".into(), "out".into()],
    inductance: 10e-6,
    saturation: Some(InductorSaturation { i_sat: 3.0 / 0.6, l_sat: 1e-6 }),
};
```

#### Sources

```rust
CircuitElement::VoltageSource { id, nodes: [String; 2], voltage: f64, waveform: Option<Waveform> }
CircuitElement::CurrentSource { id, nodes: [String; 2], current: f64, waveform: Option<Waveform> }
```

`nodes[0]` is the positive terminal for voltage sources; current flows from `nodes[0]` toward `nodes[1]` for current sources.

A `Waveform` (sine, pulse, square, triangle, PWM, PWL) on any source triggers transient analysis. See [`waveform.rs`](src/waveform.rs) for the `Waveform` enum.

#### Battery

```rust
CircuitElement::Battery { id, nodes: [String; 2], params: BatteryParams, state_of_charge: f64 }
```

`nodes` are `[positive, negative]`. The cell is an equivalent circuit: open-circuit voltage by state of charge (`params.ocv`, interpolated), behind a series resistance `r_series` and an optional RC pair (`params.rc`) for the slow sag after a load step and the recovery after it. Its terminal voltage is `OCV(SoC) − R0·i − v1`.

- **DC:** the open-circuit voltage at `state_of_charge` behind `R0 + R1`.
- **Transient:** the RC pair charges, and the state of charge falls by the charge drawn, `dSoC/dt = −i/(3600·capacity)`. Each step's `state_of_charge` (and the result's, at the end) holds it by battery id. Below 0 the cell is over-discharged and holds its 0 % voltage. A battery with an RC pair makes `solve_circuit` run a transient.
- **AC:** the impedance `R0 + R1‖C1`.

`current_through` flows `nodes[0] → nodes[1]` inside the cell, as for a voltage source, so it is negative while discharging. Presets: `BatteryParams::lithium_ion(capacity_ah, r_series)` (a typical Li-ion/LiPo rest curve, 3.27–4.20 V), `BatteryParams::cr2032()` (a 225 mAh coin cell with its pulse-recovery pair) and `BatteryParams::constant(volts, capacity_ah, r_series)`.

```rust
use sindr::battery::BatteryParams;

// A 500 mAh LiPo at 80 %, 0.15 Ω.
let cell = CircuitElement::Battery {
    id: "B1".into(),
    nodes: ["vbat".into(), "0".into()],
    params: BatteryParams::lithium_ion(0.5, 0.15),
    state_of_charge: 0.8,
};
```

#### Switches

```rust
CircuitElement::Switch     { id, nodes: [String; 2], closed: bool }
CircuitElement::Pushbutton { id, nodes: [String; 2], closed: bool }
```

Modeled as a 0.01 Ω resistor when closed, 1 GΩ when open.

#### Diodes

```rust
CircuitElement::Diode         { id, nodes: [String; 2], model: Option<DiodeModel> } // silicon (Vf ≈ 0.7 V) unless a SPICE-style model is set
CircuitElement::Led           { id, nodes: [String; 2], color: String } // "red"|"green"|"blue"|"yellow"|"white"
CircuitElement::ZenerDiode    { id, nodes: [String; 2], vz: f64 }   // breakdown voltage at 5 mA
CircuitElement::SchottkyDiode { id, nodes: [String; 2] }            // Vf ≈ 0.3 V
CircuitElement::Photodiode    { id, nodes: [String; 2], irradiance: f64 } // irradiance in W
```

All diodes use Newton-Raphson automatically when present. `Diode`'s optional `model` is what a SPICE `.model D` card fills in: `DiodeModel { is, n, rs }` (defaults `1e-14`, `1`, `0`), the junction charge `cjo`, `vj`, `m`, `fc`, `tt` (defaults `0`, `1`, `0.5`, `0.5`, `0`) and breakdown `bv`, `ibv` (defaults none, 1 mA). With `cjo` or `tt` set the diode stores charge, so it shows reverse recovery in transient and a capacitance in AC, and the circuit takes the transient path; its `current_through` then includes the charging current, while `power` stays the dissipation. `bv` adds SPICE's exponential reverse breakdown, fitted to pass `ibv` near `−bv` as ngspice does. A `ZenerDiode` is exactly such a diode: `bv = vz`, `ibv` = 5 mA (a small zener's test current) and `rs` = 1 Ω, so it matches ngspice with the card `D(IS=1e-14 N=1 RS=1 BV=vz IBV=5m)`. Each diode variant accepts an optional `temperature: f64` field (K, default 300.15 K): IS scales with the SPICE temperature formula and the thermal voltage is kT/q at that temperature.

#### Varactor diode

```rust
CircuitElement::Varactor {
    id: String,
    nodes: [String; 2],  // [anode, cathode]
    params: VaractorParams, // { cj0, phi, m }
}
```

Varactors are purely reactive — treated as open circuit in DC, as their junction capacitance at the bias point in AC, and stamped as a voltage-dependent capacitor `C_j(V) = cj0 / (1 - V/phi)^m` each transient timestep. Always triggers transient analysis.

#### Transistors

```rust
// BJT — nodes: [base, collector, emitter]
CircuitElement::Bjt {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    kind: BjtKind,                          // BjtKind::Npn or BjtKind::Pnp
    bf: f64,                                // forward beta, default 100
    temperature: f64,                       // junction temp (K), default 300.15 K
    parasitic_caps: Option<BjtParasiticCaps>, // { cbe, cbc } in Farads; None = disabled
    model: Option<BjtModel>,                // IS, BR, NF, NR, VAF; None = built-in defaults
}

// MOSFET — nodes: [gate, drain, source]; body tied to source
CircuitElement::Mosfet {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    kind: MosfetKind,                          // MosfetKind::Nmos or MosfetKind::Pmos
    params: MosfetParams,                      // KP, VTO, LAMBDA, GAMMA, PHI; VTO SPICE-signed (negative for PMOS)
    parasitic_caps: Option<MosfetParasiticCaps>, // { cgs, cgd } in Farads; None = disabled
    body_diode: Option<DiodeModel>,            // power MOSFET's body diode; None = none
}

// IGBT — nodes: [gate, collector, emitter]
CircuitElement::Igbt {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    params: IgbtParams, // { vth, k, vce_sat }
}

// JFET — nodes: [gate, drain, source]
CircuitElement::Jfet {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    kind: JfetKind, // JfetKind::NChannel or JfetKind::PChannel
    idss: f64,      // drain saturation current at Vgs = 0 (A)
    vp: f64,        // pinch-off voltage (V), negative for N-channel
}
```

A MOSFET's `body_diode` is a SPICE diode card (`DiodeModel`) from source to drain for NMOS, drain to source for PMOS. It conducts when a bridge or inductive load pulls the drain past the source with the channel off. Every analysis solves it as a `Diode` named `<id>.body`, which is where its current shows in the results; `bv` on it sets the part's avalanche voltage.

`BjtKind`, `MosfetKind`, `JfetKind`, `IgbtParams` and `VaractorParams` are re-exported from `sindr` directly. `BjtParasiticCaps` and `MosfetParasiticCaps` live in `sindr::circuit`, and `MosfetParams` in `sindr_devices::mosfet`.

When `parasitic_caps` is set, Cbe/Cbc (BJT) or Cgs/Cgd (MOSFET) are stamped as capacitor companions each transient timestep, with per-junction voltage state tracked internally, and as jωC in AC. This automatically triggers transient analysis.

**NPN common-emitter example:**

```rust
use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement, BjtKind, solve_circuit};

let circuit = Circuit {
    ground_node: "0".into(),
    components: vec![
        CircuitElement::VoltageSource {
            id: "Vcc".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "0".into()], voltage: 10.0, waveform: None,
        },
        CircuitElement::Resistor {
            id: "Rc".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "collector".into()], resistance: 1_000.0,
        },
        CircuitElement::Resistor {
            id: "Rb".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "base".into()], resistance: 470_000.0,
        },
        CircuitElement::Bjt {
            id: "Q1".into(),
            nodes: ["base".into(), "collector".into(), "0".into()],
            kind: BjtKind::Npn,
            bf: 100.0,
            temperature: 300.15,
            parasitic_caps: None,
            model: None,
        },
    ],
    ..Default::default()
};

let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;

let q1 = result.bjt_results.iter().find(|b| b.id == "Q1").unwrap();
println!("Vbe = {:.3} V, Vce = {:.3} V, Ic = {:.3} mA, region = {}",
    q1.vbe, q1.vce, q1.ic * 1000.0, q1.region);
```

#### Transformer (coupled inductors)

```rust
CircuitElement::Transformer {
    id: String,
    nodes: [String; 4],  // [p1, q1, p2, q2] — primary (p1,q1), secondary (p2,q2)
    l1: f64,             // primary inductance (H)
    l2: f64,             // secondary inductance (H)
    k: f64,              // coupling coefficient [0, 0.999]; default 0.999 (near-ideal)
}
```

Mutual inductance M = k·√(L1·L2). In DC analysis both windings are short circuits. In AC and transient, two branch current unknowns (one per winding) are added to the MNA system, so the windings are coupled through M. k=1 is mathematically singular — use k≤0.999.

#### Controlled sources

```rust
// Voltage-controlled voltage source: V_out = gain × V_ctrl
CircuitElement::Vcvs { id, nodes: [out+, out-], control_nodes: [ctrl+, ctrl-], gain: f64 }

// Voltage-controlled current source: I_out = gm × V_ctrl
CircuitElement::Vccs { id, nodes: [out_from, out_to], control_nodes: [ctrl+, ctrl-], gm: f64 }

// Current-controlled voltage source: V_out = rm × I_ctrl
CircuitElement::Ccvs { id, nodes: [out+, out-], control_source: String, rm: f64 }

// Current-controlled current source: I_out = alpha × I_ctrl
CircuitElement::Cccs { id, nodes: [out_from, out_to], control_source: String, alpha: f64 }
```

`control_source` is the `id` of the voltage source whose branch current is sensed.

#### Op-amp / Comparator

```rust
// nodes: [in_plus, in_minus, out]
CircuitElement::OpAmp      { id, nodes: [String; 3], v_pos: f64, v_neg: f64, model: Option<OpAmpModel> } // rails, default ±15 V
CircuitElement::Comparator { id, nodes: [String; 3], v_pos: f64, v_neg: f64 } // default 5 V / 0 V
```

With `model: None` both are a high-gain VCVS (gain 1×10⁵) with no frequency response, and the rails aren't enforced. An `OpAmpModel` turns the op-amp into a macromodel. It has open-loop `gain` (default 1e5), a dominant pole from `gbw` (default 1 MHz), a `slew_rate` limit (default 0.5 V/µs), `r_out`, `offset_voltage` and `bias_current`, and its output clamps to `v_pos`/`v_neg` with anti-windup. A non-inverting stage of gain G then has its −3 dB point near `gbw / G`, and a large step rises at the slew rate:

```rust
use sindr::{CircuitElement, OpAmpModel};

let u1 = CircuitElement::OpAmp {
    id: "U1".into(),
    nodes: ["in".into(), "fb".into(), "out".into()],
    v_pos: 12.0,
    v_neg: -12.0,
    model: Some(OpAmpModel { gbw: Some(3e6), slew_rate: Some(13e6), r_out: 50.0, ..OpAmpModel::default() }),
};
```

The pole and slew limit act in transient and AC runs. An op-amp doesn't count as reactive, so `solve_circuit` still runs DC for a circuit whose only dynamics are op-amps; call `solve_transient` to see them.

#### Sensors / misc

```rust
CircuitElement::Photoresistor { id, nodes: [String; 2], light_level: f64 } // 0.0 (dark, ~1 MΩ) – 1.0 (bright, ~1 kΩ)
CircuitElement::Thermistor    { id, nodes: [String; 2], temperature: f64 } // Kelvin, default 298.15 K (25 °C)
CircuitElement::Potentiometer { id, nodes: [top, wiper, bottom], resistance: f64, position: f64 } // position 0.0–1.0
CircuitElement::Relay {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 4],     // [coil+, coil-, contact1, contact2]
    coil_resistance: f64,
    pickup_voltage: f64,
    inductance: f64,        // coil inductance (H); 0.0 = purely resistive (default)
}
CircuitElement::Fuse             { id, nodes: [String; 2], rating: f64, blown: bool } // 1 mΩ intact, 1 GΩ blown; rating is display-only
CircuitElement::VoltageRegulator { id, nodes: [input, output, gnd], voltage: f64, model: Option<RegulatorParams> }
```

When `inductance > 0`, the relay coil is modeled as an RL circuit in transient analysis (L stamped as an inductor companion). This triggers transient automatically.

`VoltageRegulator` is a linear regulator. With headroom it holds `voltage` above its ground pin; without it the output follows the input down by the dropout; past the current limit it holds the current, short circuits included. It draws its output current plus its quiescent current from the input. `model: None` is ideal (no dropout, no quiescent current, no limit) but still never puts out more than it gets in. `RegulatorParams` sets `dropout` (V, plus `dropout_resistance` Ω for one that grows with load), `quiescent_current`, `current_limit`, `line_regulation` (V/V) and `output_resistance` (Ω, load regulation). `RegulatorParams::lm7805()` and `RegulatorParams::ams1117()` are datasheet presets. Its result is the pass element: `voltage_across` is `Vin − Vout`, `current_through` the output current, and `power` the dissipation `(Vin − Vout)·Iout + Vin·Iq`, which the ratings checks and self-heating use. In AC, input ripple reaches the output through line regulation (all of it in dropout). Foldback and thermal shutdown are not modelled.

### Reading results

`solve_circuit` returns `Result<SimulationResult, SimError>`.

```rust
pub struct SimulationResult {
    pub node_voltages:    HashMap<String, f64>,  // every node including ground (0.0)
    pub branch_currents:  HashMap<String, f64>,  // voltage source branch currents by id
    pub component_results: Vec<ComponentResult>, // V, I, P for every component
    pub bjt_results:      Vec<BjtResult>,        // present only if circuit has BJTs
    pub mosfet_results:   Vec<MosfetResult>,     // present only if circuit has MOSFETs
    pub op_amp_results:   Vec<OpAmpResult>,      // present only if circuit has op-amps
    pub relay_results:    Vec<RelayResult>,      // present only if circuit has relays
    pub transient:        Option<TransientData>, // present only for reactive/waveform circuits
}

pub struct ComponentResult {
    pub id:              String,
    pub voltage_across:  f64,
    pub current_through: f64,
    pub power:           f64,
}

pub struct BjtResult {
    pub id: String, pub vbe: f64, pub vce: f64,
    pub ib: f64, pub ic: f64, pub ie: f64,
    pub power: f64, pub region: String, // "active" | "saturation" | "cutoff"
}

pub struct MosfetResult {
    pub id: String, pub vgs: f64, pub vds: f64,
    pub id_current: f64, pub power: f64, pub region: String, // "cutoff" | "triode" | "saturation"
}
```

For transient circuits, `result.transient` contains a time series. `solve_circuit` picks the duration (5 τ) and step (τ/50) from the circuit's time constants; to set them yourself, as SPICE's `.tran tstep tstop` does, use `solve_transient`:

```rust,ignore
use sindr::{solve_transient, TransientConfig};

// 10 ms in 1 µs steps; optionally cap the step with .with_tmax(…)
let result = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(10e-3, 1e-6))?;
```

Each snapshot is the end of one step, with sources evaluated at that time; the last is at `tstop`. The default integrator is Gear-2 (second order, no ringing); `.with_method(IntegrationMethod::Trapezoidal)` keeps an LC tank's amplitude exactly, and `IntegrationMethod::BackwardEuler` matches sindr before 0.1.0-alpha.7. Every method takes its first step as backward Euler.

A run starts switched on at t = 0 by default: capacitors uncharged and inductors at 0 A, unless `.with_initial_voltages(…)` or `.with_initial_current(…)` say otherwise (SPICE's `.ic` with `UIC`), so power-on inrush shows. `.with_start(TransientStart::OperatingPoint)` starts from the DC operating point instead, as SPICE's `.tran` without `UIC` does: each source at its t = 0 value, capacitors charged and inductors and transformer windings carrying its currents, with any initial voltages and currents held while it's solved. A SPICE deck's `ParsedNetlist::transient_config()` sets the run up the way ngspice does: the start, `.ic`, `tmax`, and `tstart` (`.with_tstart(t)`: integrate from 0, keep the steps from `t` on).

Steps are at most `tstep` long and every multiple of `tstep` gets a snapshot. In between, the stepper shortens steps where the local truncation error would exceed SPICE's default tolerances, and lands exactly on each corner of a source waveform (pulse edges, PWL points, square-wave flips), so a 1 ns edge in a 1 ms run is resolved without 1 ns steps everywhere. `result.transient.stats` counts accepted and rejected steps; `.with_fixed_step()` turns the error control off.


```rust
pub struct TransientData {
    pub timesteps: Vec<TimestepSnapshot>,
    pub time_step: f64,
    pub duration:  f64,
}

pub struct TimestepSnapshot {
    pub time:              f64,
    pub node_voltages:     HashMap<String, f64>,
    pub component_results: Vec<ComponentResult>,
}
```

#### CSV export

`TransientData`, `AcResult`, `DcSweepResult` and `TempSweepResult` each have `to_csv()`. It writes one row per point: the scale first (`time`, `frequency`, the swept source's id, or `temperature` in K), then `v(<node>)` for each node in name order, then `i(<id>)` (each component's `current_through`) in circuit order. AC writes each node as `re(v(<node>))` and `im(v(<node>))`. Numbers read back as the same `f64`, and names with commas or quotes are quoted.

```rust
std::fs::write("rc.csv", result.transient.unwrap().to_csv())?;
```

### AC analysis

Small-signal frequency response around the DC operating point. Nonlinear devices are linearised at the operating point, then each frequency is a complex MNA solve.

```rust
use sindr::ac_analysis::{solve_ac, AcConfig, FrequencySpacing};

let config = AcConfig {
    f_start: 1.0,
    f_stop: 100_000.0,
    num_points: 51,
    spacing: FrequencySpacing::Logarithmic, // or Linear
    source_id: "V1".into(),                 // voltage source that carries the AC stimulus
    ac_magnitude: 1.0,
};
let result = solve_ac(&circuit, &config)?;

let gain = result.gain_curve("n_out");   // (Hz, dB)
let phase = result.phase_curve("n_out"); // (Hz, degrees)
```

`num_points` counts both endpoints; with 1, only `f_start` is solved. Invalid configs (0 points, non-finite values, `f_start > f_stop`, `f_start <= 0` with logarithmic spacing) return `SimError::InvalidComponent`.

### Transfer function

SPICE's `.tf`: the small-signal DC gain from an input source to an output, the resistance the input source sees, and the output resistance, all at the DC operating point (capacitors open, inductors shorted, nonlinear devices linearised).

```rust
use sindr::{solve_tf, TfConfig, TfOutput};

let config = TfConfig {
    output: TfOutput::Voltage { node: "out".into(), reference: None }, // or TfOutput::Current { source_id }
    input_source: "V1".into(),                                         // a voltage or current source
};
let tf = solve_tf(&circuit, &config)?;
println!("{} V/V, Rin {} Ω, Rout {} Ω", tf.gain, tf.input_resistance, tf.output_resistance);
```

The input resistance is infinite when the input source draws no small-signal current. Every other independent source is zeroed for the output resistance. A current output (`I(Vx)`) runs from the source's `nodes[0]` through it to `nodes[1]`, as SPICE's.

### DC sensitivity

SPICE's `.sens`: the derivative of one DC output with respect to each component parameter, at the operating point. One adjoint solve covers them all, however many there are.

```rust
use sindr::{solve_sensitivity, SensConfig, TfOutput};

let config = SensConfig {
    output: TfOutput::Voltage { node: "out".into(), reference: None }, // or TfOutput::Current { source_id }
};
let sens = solve_sensitivity(&circuit, &config)?;

for e in &sens.entries {
    println!("{}: {} per unit, {} per +1 %", e.component_id, e.sensitivity, e.per_percent);
}
```

Entries cover resistance, voltage and current source values, VCVS gain and VCCS gm. Other components get no entry: device-model parameters, CCVS and CCCS gains, capacitors and inductors. There is no AC sensitivity.

### Noise

SPICE's `.noise`: thermal noise of resistances and FET channels, shot noise of junction currents, and flicker (1/f) noise where a model sets `KF`, at an output voltage and referred back to an input source. One adjoint solve per frequency gives every source's share.

```rust
use sindr::{solve_noise, NoiseConfig};
use sindr::ac_analysis::FrequencySpacing;

let noise = solve_noise(&circuit, &NoiseConfig {
    output: "out".into(),
    reference: None,
    input_source: "V1".into(),
    f_start: 10.0,
    f_stop: 100e3,
    num_points: 41,
    spacing: FrequencySpacing::Logarithmic,
})?;

println!("{:.2} µV rms at the output", noise.total_output_noise * 1e6);
for (source, total) in noise.sources.iter().zip(&noise.source_totals) {
    println!("  {} ({:?}): {:.2} µV", source.component, source.kind, total * 1e6);
}
```

Each point has the output and input-referred densities (`output_density()`, `input_density()`, per √Hz) and each source's contribution. The totals integrate over the band as ngspice does. Noise is at 27 °C. Sources, controlled sources, op-amps, regulators and a diode's series resistance are noiseless.

### DC sweep

Sweep a voltage or current source across a range and collect operating points at each step. Each point's Newton–Raphson starts from the one before, as in SPICE.

```rust
use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement, dc_sweep};

let sweep = dc_sweep(&circuit, "V1", 0.0, 5.0, 51)?;

let v_curve = sweep.node_voltage_curve("n2");
let i_curve = sweep.component_current_curve("D1");
```

Two sources, one inside the other (SPICE's `.dc VDS 0 5 0.1 VGS 0 3 0.5`), draw a family of device curves: one `DcSweepResult` along the inner source per value of the outer one.

```rust
use sindr::{dc_sweep_nested, dc_sweep::DcSweepAxis};

let family = dc_sweep_nested(
    &circuit,
    &DcSweepAxis::from_step("VDS", 0.0, 5.0, 0.1)?, // inner, fastest
    &DcSweepAxis::from_step("VGS", 0.0, 3.0, 0.5)?, // outer
)?;
for curve in &family.curves {
    let id_vs_vds = curve.sweep.component_current_curve("M1");
    println!("VGS = {} V: {} points", curve.outer_value, id_vs_vds.len());
}
```

A parsed `.dc` card gives its axes with `analysis.dc_axes()`.

### Temperature sweep

Solve a circuit at a series of junction temperatures and collect operating points. Useful for BJT Ic vs. temperature curves and thermal characterisation.

```rust
use sindr::{Circuit, temperature_sweep, TempSweepResult};

// All junction devices (BJT, diode, LED, Zener, Schottky, Photodiode) have their
// temperature field overridden at each step.
let result = temperature_sweep(&circuit, 250.0, 350.0, 11)?; // 250 K → 350 K, 11 points

for point in &result.points {
    println!("T = {:.1} K, Ic = {:.3} mA", point.temperature,
        point.bjt_results.iter().find(|b| b.id == "Q1").map_or(0.0, |b| b.ic) * 1000.0);
}
```

```rust
pub struct TempSweepResult {
    pub points: Vec<TempSweepPoint>,
}

pub struct TempSweepPoint {
    pub temperature:      f64,
    pub node_voltages:    HashMap<String, f64>,
    pub component_results: Vec<ComponentResult>,
    pub bjt_results:      Vec<BjtResult>,
}
```

`num_steps` must be ≥ 2, and both temperatures finite and above 0 K.

### Self-heating

Give a part a thermal path and the solver heats its junction by what it dissipates, then feeds that temperature back into the device: IS and kT/q for diodes, LEDs, Zeners, Schottkys, photodiodes and BJTs, and the resistance of a thermistor. The DC solve iterates until power and temperature agree. A transient carries a thermal RC state per part (`Cθ·dT/dt = P − (T − ambient)/Rθ`), starting cold at ambient.

```rust
use sindr::{solve_circuit, Part, SimError, Thermal};

// SOT-23 on its own (~500 K/W), or a TO-220 on a heatsink.
circuit.parts.insert("Q2".into(), Part { thermal: Some(Thermal::junction_to_ambient(500.0)), ..Part::default() });
circuit.parts.insert("Q3".into(), Part { thermal: Some(Thermal::on_heatsink(5.0, 10.0)), ..Part::default() });

match solve_circuit(&circuit) {
    Ok(result) => println!("Tj(Q2) = {:.1} K", result.junction_temperatures["Q2"]),
    Err(SimError::ThermalRunaway { part, temperature }) => println!("{part} runs away past {temperature:.0} K"),
    Err(e) => return Err(e),
}
```

`Thermal` takes `rth_ja` (K/W), or `rth_jc` plus `rth_ca` for a part on a heatsink, an optional `cth` (J/K; without it a transient's junction follows its power with no lag), and `ambient` (K, default 300.15). With it, the element's own `temperature` field is ignored. `SimulationResult::junction_temperatures` and each `TimestepSnapshot`'s carry the result, and `Ratings::tj_max` is checked against them. When no balance exists (a junction past 1000 K, or the iteration never settles), the solve returns `SimError::ThermalRunaway`. MOSFETs, JFETs, IGBTs and resistors report a junction temperature, but their models don't depend on it.

### Ratings checks

Check a solved circuit against each part's absolute maximum ratings, so nothing gets powered past its datasheet limits. Ratings live on the component's `Part` (`circuit.parts`, keyed by component id). `check_ratings` looks at the DC operating point, or at every step of a transient, where inrush, inductive kickback and start-up peaks show up.

```rust
use sindr::{check_ratings, solve_transient, Part, Ratings, RatingStatus, TransientConfig};

circuit.parts.insert("Q1".into(), Part {
    ratings: Ratings { vce: Some(45.0), ic: Some(0.1), power: Some(0.5), ..Ratings::default() },
    ..Part::default()
});

let result = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(1e-3, 1e-6))?;
let report = check_ratings(&circuit, &result)?;
for c in report.exceeded() {
    println!("{} {:?}: {:.3} {} at t = {:?} (limit {:?}, margin {:.0}%)",
        c.part, c.rating, c.worst.unwrap(), c.rating.unit(), c.time, c.limit,
        c.margin_percent.unwrap_or(f64::NAN));
}
assert!(report.is_safe()); // false while anything is exceeded *or* unverified
```

Each component kind has ratings it needs, checked whether set or not; a missing one is `RatingStatus::Unverified`, never a pass:

| Component | Needs |
|---|---|
| resistor, potentiometer, thermistor, photoresistor | `power` |
| capacitor | `voltage` |
| inductor | `current` |
| diode, Schottky, LED, photodiode | `reverse_voltage`, `forward_current`, `power` |
| Zener | `power` |
| varactor | `reverse_voltage` |
| BJT | `vce`, `vcb`, `veb`, `ic`, `power` |
| MOSFET, JFET | `vds`, `vgs`, `id`, `power` |
| IGBT | `vce`, `vgs` (gate–emitter), `ic`, `power` |
| anything with `Part::thermal` | also `tj_max` |

Any other rating set on a part is checked too: `power`, `voltage` and `current` on any component (on the port its `ComponentResult` reports), the rest on the devices they belong to. All limits are magnitudes, so PNP and PMOS parts use the same positive numbers. Transistor power is `|V·I|` on the Vce/Ic or Vds/Id port, without base or gate dissipation.

### Measurements and specs

Turn a result into numbers, and the numbers into a verdict. A `Measurement` reads a `Signal` (`v(out)`, `v(a, b)`, `i(R1)`, in dB or phase on AC) off any result: a transient, AC, DC or temperature sweep, or an operating point. A `Spec` adds limits, and `check_specs` reports each one's value, limits, pass/fail and margin.

```rust
use sindr::measure::{check_specs, Crossing, Measure, Measurement, Signal, Spec, Stat};

let tran = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(10e-3, 1e-6))?;
let specs = [
    Spec::new(Measurement::new("vout", Measure::stat(Signal::v("out"), Stat::Avg)).window(5e-3, 10e-3))
        .between(4.9, 5.1),
    Spec::new(Measurement::new("ripple", Measure::stat(Signal::v("out"), Stat::PeakToPeak)).window(5e-3, 10e-3))
        .at_most(0.05),
    Spec::new(Measurement::new("settle", Measure::settling(Signal::v("out"), 0.05))).at_most(2e-3),
];
let report = check_specs(&tran, &specs).with_ratings(check_ratings(&circuit, &tran)?);
for c in report.failed() {
    println!("{}: {:?} outside {:?}..{:?} by {:?}", c.name, c.value, c.min, c.max, c.margin);
}
assert!(report.passed()); // every spec passed and every part is within its ratings
```

| `Measure` | SPICE `.meas` | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| `Find { at }` | `FIND v(out) AT=1m` | value at x, interpolated |
| `Stat` | `AVG`, `RMS`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `PP`, `INTEG` (and `Final`) | statistic over the window (`FROM=`/`TO=`) |
| `When(Crossing)` | `WHEN v(out)=2.5 RISE=2` | x of the nth rising, falling or any crossing, or the last |
| `Delay { trig, targ }` | `TRIG … VAL= … TARG … VAL=` | x(targ) − x(trig) |
| `Transition` | | rise or fall time between fractions of the swing (10–90 %) |
| `Settling { band }` | | time from the window start until it stays within ±band of its final value |
| `Bandwidth { drop_db }` | `WHEN vdb(out)=-3 FALL=1` | first x after the peak `drop_db` below it (−3 dB point) |

A measurement that can't be taken (an unknown node, a level never crossed, a phase on a transient) is `SpecStatus::Unmeasured` with a reason, never a pass; `Measurement::on` returns it as `SimError::Measurement`. Average and RMS are weighted by step width, so the transient's uneven steps don't skew them. With the `spice` feature, `.meas tran|ac|dc` cards land in `ParsedNetlist::measurements`, each with the analysis it measures.

### Examples

One small program per capability in [`examples/`](./examples), run with `cargo run -p sindr --example <name>`:

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| `voltage_divider` | Linear DC operating point |
| `bjt_amplifier` | Nonlinear DC with a BJT |
| `transient_rc` | Transient step response |
| `bode_plot` | AC analysis |
| `transfer_function` | Transfer function (`.tf`) |
| `sensitivity` | DC sensitivity (`.sens`) |
| `dc_sweep_diode` | DC sweep (diode I–V curve) |
| `temperature_sweep` | Temperature sweep |
| `initial_voltages` | Seeding Newton–Raphson (`.nodeset`) |
| `parse_netlist` | SPICE input (`--features spice`) |
| `list_examples`, `run_example` | The built-in named circuits |

### Error handling

```rust
pub enum SimError {
    NoGround,
    DisconnectedNodes(Vec<String>),
    FloatingNode(String),
    SingularMatrix,
    InvalidSolution,
    InvalidComponent(String),
    InvalidResistance(String),
    ConvergenceFailed { iterations: usize, max_step_volts: f64 },
}
```

`ConvergenceFailed` means Newton-Raphson did not converge — usually caused by a nonlinear circuit with no DC path to ground, or component values far outside typical operating ranges. The `max_step_volts` field gives the largest per-node Newton step (V) on the final iteration, useful for distinguishing slow convergence from genuine divergence. (Note: this is a step magnitude `max_i |V_new[i] − V_prev[i]|`, not a KCL residual `|F(x)|`.)

### Solver routing

`solve_circuit` picks a path automatically — you never select it manually:

| Circuit contains | Solver used |
|---|---|
| Only linear elements | Direct MNA (LU factorisation) |
| Nonlinear elements (diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs, IGBTs…) | Newton-Raphson iteration |
| Reactive elements (C, L, Varactor, Transformer, parasitic caps, a diode whose model sets `cjo` or `tt`) or waveform sources | Transient (Gear-2 by default) |
| Both reactive and nonlinear | Transient with per-step Newton-Raphson |

The transient solver steps up to `tstep` (or `tmax`, if smaller), shortens a step where the local truncation error would exceed SPICE's default tolerances (RELTOL 1e-3, VNTOL 1 µV, TRTOL 7), and lands exactly on every corner of a source waveform. A step whose Newton-Raphson solve fails is halved and retried.

### Performance

Medians from `cargo bench -p sindr --bench transient --bench newton` on an Apple M1 Pro (release build, one thread). The circuits are in `sindr/benches/`.

| Case | 10 | 100 | 1 000 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DC, diode–resistor chain (devices) | 37 µs | 0.93 ms | 8.7 ms |
| DC, cascaded BJT common-emitter stages (devices) | 0.18 ms | 6.7 ms | 440 ms |
| Transient, RC ladder over 200 steps (stages) | 0.95 ms | 15 ms | 143 ms |

A 50 Hz half-wave rectifier with a filter cap over five cycles (5 000 steps) takes 9 ms. The cascaded BJT row grows faster than linearly, because each stage's bias depends on the one before it and Newton needs more iterations as the chain lengthens. `benches/mna_solve.rs` has the raw dense and sparse solve times up to 10 000 nodes.

Pull requests run these benchmarks against their base on the same runner, and CI fails if any case is more than 25 % slower.

### Serde

With the default `serde` feature, `Circuit` and `SimulationResult` (and all nested types) implement `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Component types use snake_case tags:

```json
{
  "ground_node": "0",
  "components": [
    { "type": "voltage_source", "id": "V1", "nodes": ["n1", "0"], "voltage": 10.0 },
    { "type": "resistor",       "id": "R1", "nodes": ["n1", "0"], "resistance": 1000.0 },
    { "type": "bjt",  "id": "Q1", "nodes": ["b", "c", "e"], "kind": "npn", "bf": 100 },
    { "type": "transformer", "id": "T1", "nodes": ["p1","q1","p2","q2"], "l1": 1e-3, "l2": 4e-3 },
    { "type": "varactor", "id": "D1", "nodes": ["a", "k"], "params": { "cj0": 10e-12, "phi": 0.7, "m": 0.5 } }
  ]
}
```

Fields with defaults (`bf`, `temperature`, `k`, `coil_resistance`, `position`, `v_pos`, `v_neg`, `parasitic_caps`) can be omitted from JSON and will take their defaults.


# Crate `sindr-core` README (sindr-core/README.md)

## sindr-core

[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/sindr-core.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/sindr-core)
[![docs.rs](https://docs.rs/sindr-core/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/sindr-core)

The circuit and design data model behind [`sindr`](https://crates.io/crates/sindr), without the solver. It holds `Circuit`, every `CircuitElement`, `Waveform`, and the design layer: blocks and instances, net scoping, and part data (reference, value, symbol, footprint). It depends on `sindr-devices` (device parameter types), `thiserror` and optional `serde`. There is no linear algebra.

Use it to build, store or exchange circuits in a design tool. `sindr` re-exports all of it, so `sindr::Circuit` is the same type and simulates directly.

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr-core = "0.1.0-alpha.8"
```

### Hierarchy

A `Block` is a reusable definition, what `.subckt` is in SPICE. An `Instance` places one and binds its ports to the caller's nets. Inside a block a net is a port, ground, a global (`Circuit::globals`) or local to each instance. `Circuit::flatten` expands it all, naming elements and local nets with the instance path (`X1.R1`, `X1.mid`). sindr's analyses flatten for you.

```rust
use sindr_core::{Block, Circuit, CircuitElement, Instance, Part};

let r = |id: &str, a: &str, b: &str| CircuitElement::Resistor {
    id: id.into(),
    nodes: [a.into(), b.into()],
    resistance: 1e3,
};

let mut circuit = Circuit::new(
    "0",
    vec![CircuitElement::VoltageSource {
        id: "V1".into(),
        nodes: ["in".into(), "0".into()],
        voltage: 10.0,
        waveform: None,
    }],
);
circuit.blocks.insert(
    "divider".into(),
    Block {
        ports: vec!["top".into(), "out".into()],
        components: vec![r("R1", "top", "out"), r("R2", "out", "0")],
        ..Block::default()
    },
);
circuit.instances.push(Instance::new("X1", "divider", ["in", "mid"]));
circuit.parts.insert(
    "V1".into(),
    Part { symbol: Some("Simulation_SPICE:VDC".into()), ..Part::default() },
);

let flat = circuit.flatten().unwrap();
let ids: Vec<&str> = flat.components.iter().map(|c| c.id()).collect();
assert_eq!(ids, ["V1", "X1.R1", "X1.R2"]);
```

`Part` data is ignored by the simulator, except `Part::ratings`: absolute maximum `Ratings` that `sindr::check_ratings` compares a simulation against. Empty hierarchy and part fields are left out of JSON, so a flat circuit serialises exactly as before.

### License

MIT OR Apache-2.0.


# Crate `sindr-devices` README (sindr-devices/README.md)

## sindr-devices

Pure electronics device physics companion models for MNA circuit simulation.

`sindr-devices` is a standalone workspace crate that implements the nonlinear device models used by the `sindr` solver. It has no dependency on the solver — pure physics math, independently testable.

### Devices

| Module | Device | Model |
|--------|--------|-------|
| `diode` | Silicon diode | Shockley companion with series resistance, temperature IS scaling, SPICE `BV`/`IBV` breakdown and junction charge (`CJO`, `VJ`, `M`, `FC`, `TT`) |
| `bjt` | BJT (NPN/PNP) | Ebers-Moll companion with Early voltage |
| `mosfet` | MOSFET (NMOS/PMOS) | Level-1 companion; body effect when called with a `vbs` (in a sindr circuit the body is tied to the source) |
| `jfet` | JFET (N/P-channel) | Shichman-Hodges |
| `igbt` | IGBT | MOSFET square-law collector current, blocks reverse V_CE |
| `led` | LED | Diode with colour-dependent forward voltage |
| `zener` | Zener diode | Shockley plus reverse-breakdown branch |
| `schottky` | Schottky diode | Shockley with Schottky IS/N (~0.3 V forward) |
| `varactor` | Varactor diode | Voltage-dependent junction capacitance C_j(V) |
| `thermistor` | NTC thermistor | Beta model R(T) = R₀·exp(β·(1/T − 1/T₀)) |
| `regulator` | Linear voltage regulator | Piecewise linear: dropout, quiescent current, current limit, line and load regulation; LM7805 and AMS1117 presets |
| `photodiode` | Photodiode | Diode + photocurrent offset |
| `photoresistor` | Photoresistor (LDR) | Light-level-dependent resistance |

### Usage

Add to your `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr-devices = "0.1.0-alpha.8"
```

Two-terminal companions return `(g_eq, i_eq)`: the linearised conductance (S)
and the Norton current source (A) at the operating point. Multi-terminal
devices return a companion struct.

#### Diode

```rust
use sindr_devices::diode::{diode_companion, temperature_scale_is, DiodeParams};

let params = DiodeParams::silicon(); // IS=1e-14, N=1.0, rs=0.0, 300.15 K
let (g_eq, i_eq) = diode_companion(0.65, &params);
assert!(g_eq > 0.0);

// Temperature-scaled IS (SPICE formula): IS, T, Tnom, Eg, XTI, N
let is_at_125c = temperature_scale_is(1e-14, 398.15, 300.15, 1.11, 3.0, 1.0);
assert!(is_at_125c > 1e-14);
```

`DiodeParams` fields: `is` (A), `n` (ideality), `rs` (series resistance, Ω),
`temperature` (K).

#### BJT

```rust
use sindr_devices::bjt::{bjt_companion, BjtParams};

let params = BjtParams::new(100.0); // BF=100, IS=1e-14, no Early effect
let c = bjt_companion(0.65, -5.0, &params); // Vbe, Vbc
// c.g_be, c.g_bc, c.g_ce (Early output conductance, 0 when vaf = 0), c.ic, c.ib
assert!(c.ic > 0.0);
```

`BjtParams` fields: `is`, `bf`, `nf`, `br`, `nr`, `vaf` / `var` (Early
voltages, V; 0.0 = infinite), `temperature` (K).

#### MOSFET

```rust
use sindr_devices::mosfet::{mosfet_companion, MosfetParams};

let params = MosfetParams::default_nmos(); // or default_pmos()
let c = mosfet_companion(2.0, 3.0, 0.0, &params); // Vgs, Vds, Vbs
// c.id, c.gm, c.gds, c.gmb (body effect), c.vth, c.region
assert!(c.id > 0.0);
```

#### JFET

```rust
use sindr_devices::jfet::{jfet_companion, JfetKind};

let c = jfet_companion(-0.5, 5.0, JfetKind::NChannel, 10e-3, -2.0); // Vgs, Vds, kind, IDSS, Vp
// c.gm, c.gds, c.i_eq
assert!(c.gm > 0.0);
```

#### IGBT

```rust
use sindr_devices::igbt::{igbt_companion, IgbtParams};

let params = IgbtParams::default(); // vth=5.0, k=5.0
let c = igbt_companion(10.0, 5.0, &params); // Vge, Vce
// c.gm = ∂Ids/∂Vge, c.g_ce = ∂Ids/∂Vce, c.ids, c.i_eq
assert!(c.ids > 0.0);
```

#### Varactor

```rust
use sindr_devices::varactor::{junction_capacitance, varactor_companion, VaractorParams};

let params = VaractorParams { cj0: 10e-12, phi: 0.7, m: 0.5 };
let c_j = junction_capacitance(-2.0, &params); // reverse-biased capacitance (F)
assert!(c_j < params.cj0);

// Backward Euler companion from the previous timestep's voltage; dt = 0.0 gives a DC open circuit.
let (g_eq, i_eq) = varactor_companion(-2.0, 1e-6, &params);
```

#### Other diodes and sensors

```rust
use sindr_devices::led::{led_params, LedColor};
use sindr_devices::photodiode::{photodiode_companion, PhotodiodeParams};
use sindr_devices::photoresistor::{ldr_resistance, PhotoresistorParams};
use sindr_devices::schottky::{schottky_companion, SchottkyParams};
use sindr_devices::thermistor::{thermistor_resistance, ThermistorParams};
use sindr_devices::zener::{zener_companion, ZenerParams};

let red = led_params(LedColor::Red); // DiodeParams for use with diode_companion
let (g, i) = schottky_companion(0.3, &SchottkyParams::default()); // IS=1e-8, N=1.0
let (g, i) = zener_companion(-5.5, &ZenerParams::new(5.1)); // Vz = 5.1 V
let (g, i) = photodiode_companion(-1.0, 0.1, &PhotodiodeParams::default()); // 0.1 W irradiance

let r_85c = thermistor_resistance(358.15, &ThermistorParams::ntc_10k()); // ~2.5 kΩ
let r_dim = ldr_resistance(0.5, &PhotoresistorParams::default()); // 0.0 dark – 1.0 bright
assert!(r_85c < 10_000.0 && r_dim > 1_000.0);
```

### Optional features

| Feature | Enables |
|---------|---------|
| `serde` | `Serialize`/`Deserialize` on all param structs |

```toml
sindr-devices = { version = "0.1.0-alpha.8", features = ["serde"] }
```


# Scope and limitations (LIMITATIONS.md)

## Scope & Limitations

sindr is an **analog circuit simulator**: a SPICE-style MNA solver with semiconductor companion models, written in pure Rust. This document is the honest counterpart to the READMEs — it lists capabilities sindr does **not** have today, so you can decide whether it fits your use case before investing.

Status: pre-release alpha (`0.1.0-alpha.8`). Anything below may change.

### What sindr is

- DC, nonlinear DC (Newton-Raphson), transient (Gear-2 (default), trapezoidal or backward Euler), AC, DC sweep, temperature sweep
- Passives, sources, switches, controlled sources, op-amp / comparator macromodels, transformer
- Diode family (Si, LED, Zener, Schottky, photodiode, varactor), BJT (Ebers-Moll), MOSFET (Level-1), IGBT, JFET
- Thermistor, photoresistor, potentiometer, relay, fuse, linear voltage regulator (dropout, quiescent current, current limit, line and load regulation), battery (open-circuit voltage by state of charge, series resistance, optional RC pair)
- Programmatic Rust API + serde JSON for circuits and results

If your problem is "given an analog topology built in Rust, what are the node voltages and branch currents (possibly over time, frequency, or temperature)?", sindr is in scope.

### Out of scope (by design, today)

These are non-goals for the current crate split. They may live in sibling crates later, but they will not appear in `sindr` itself.

| Area | Status |
|------|--------|
| Digital logic simulation (gates, flip-flops, clocked sequential, event-driven kernel) | Out of scope |
| HDL ingestion (Verilog, VHDL, SystemVerilog, Verilog-A, VHDL-AMS, SystemC-AMS) | Out of scope |
| Microcontroller / instruction-set simulation | Out of scope |
| PCB layout, routing, parasitics extraction | Out of scope |
| Schematic capture GUI | Out of scope |
| Electromagnetic / field solvers (FEM, FDTD, method-of-moments) | Out of scope |
| Mechanical / multi-physics co-simulation | Out of scope |

For embedded-system design, the practical implication is that sindr can simulate the **analog portions** of a board (power stages, sensor front-ends, signal conditioning, filters) but not the digital MCU + firmware behaviour. Co-simulation with a digital tool is not supported.

### Not yet supported, but in scope

These are gaps a SPICE user would reasonably expect. They are plausible additions; none are committed.

#### Netlist & ecosystem

- **SPICE netlist import: partial.** The optional `spice` feature (`sindr::spice`) parses a practical subset of SPICE3f5 decks — R, L, C, V, I, D, Q, X, plus `.subckt`, `.model`, `.tran`, `.dc`, `.ac`, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.op`, `.ic`, `.nodeset`, `.param`, `.include`, `.lib` — into a `Circuit`. Full SPICE3 coverage and behavioural (`B`) sources are **not** implemented. `.model` cards are read only for what sindr's models have: `IS`, `N`, `RS`, `CJO`, `VJ`, `M`, `FC`, `TT`, `BV`, `IBV`, `KF`, `AF` on diodes and `IS`, `BF`, `BR`, `NF`, `NR`, `VAF`, `KF`, `AF` on BJTs. Anything else (temperature coefficients such as `EG`/`XTI`, BJT junction capacitance, Gummel–Poon high-injection terms) is rejected in strict mode and ignored with a warning in lenient mode. Vendor model libraries (TI, Infineon, ON Semi, Wolfspeed, etc.) that rely on BSIM / Gummel-Poon model cards remain unreachable.
- **SPICE netlist export: partial.** `sindr::spice::to_netlist` writes R, L, C, V, I, D, Q, E, G, F, H and transformers (as L–L–K), plus exact equivalents for switches, fuses, potentiometers, photoresistors, thermistors, LEDs and Schottky diodes. MOSFET, JFET, IGBT, zener, op-amp, comparator, relay, photodiode, varactor and regulator have no export, and neither does a junction away from 27 °C or a BJT with parasitic capacitances. No analysis cards are written. sindr's parser reads back only the R, L, C, V, I, D, Q part.
- **Hierarchy: definitions with evaluated values only.** `Circuit` has blocks, instances, global nets and part data (`sindr-core`), and the `spice` parser keeps `.subckt` structure. Blocks hold evaluated values, not parameter expressions, so a subckt whose instances bind different `.param`s becomes one block per distinct body (`name`, `name_2`, …). Reference designators are per block definition, with no per-instance annotation. The parser doesn't read `.global`, although export writes it.
- **Model cards: Shockley and Ebers–Moll subsets only.** `Diode` and `Bjt` take a `DiodeModel` / `BjtModel` (which a SPICE `.model` card fills in), but there are no BSIM / Gummel-Poon / VBIC / HICUM models, and MOSFET, JFET and the other devices take only their Rust parameter structs. A manufacturer card matches sindr's behaviour only when it uses no parameters beyond those. A diode's charge sits across its terminals in transient, at the junction voltage the diode current sets across RS; the drop the charging current itself makes across RS is left out, which matters only for large RS. AC is exact (RS in series with the junction). CJO and VJ don't scale with temperature, and the reverse leakage between 0 and breakdown is Shockley's `−IS` rather than ngspice's cubic. The BJT's Early effect (`VAF`) is `ic·(1 + vce/VAF)`, not SPICE's Gummel–Poon base charge, and `VAR` isn't modelled.
- **No Verilog-A / behavioural device language.** Adding a new device means writing a Rust companion model.

#### Analyses

| Analysis | Supported | Notes |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| `.op` (operating point) | ✅ | via `solve_circuit` |
| `.dc` (DC sweep) | ✅ | one source (`dc_sweep`) or two nested (`dc_sweep_nested`), voltage or current |
| `.tran` (transient) | ✅ | Gear-2, trapezoidal or backward Euler (`solve_transient`). Steps up to `tstep`, shortened by local truncation error and landing on waveform breakpoints. `tstart` keeps the result from there on |
| `.ac` (small-signal AC) | ✅ | swept frequency response |
| `.tf` (transfer function) | ✅ | DC small-signal gain, input and output resistance (`solve_tf`) |
| `.temp` (temperature sweep) | ✅ | junction-device temp parameter |
| `.noise` (noise analysis) | ✅ | thermal, shot and flicker (`solve_noise`), at 27 °C. Op-amps, regulators, controlled sources and a diode's `RS` are noiseless; no BJT base-resistance noise |
| `.disto` / harmonic distortion | ❌ | |
| `.pz` (pole-zero) | ❌ | |
| `.sens` (sensitivity) | ⚠️ | DC only (`solve_sensitivity`), for resistance, source values, VCVS gain and VCCS gm. No device-model parameters, CCVS or CCCS gains, or AC sensitivity |
| Monte Carlo / worst-case / corner analysis | ❌ | no parameter-distribution sampling |
| `.fft` on transient output | ❌ | user-side only |
| `.meas` (measurements) | ⚠️ | `sindr::measure`: statistics, `FIND … AT`, `WHEN`, `TRIG`/`TARG`, plus rise/fall, settling and −3 dB in the API. No `FIND … WHEN`, `DERIV` or `PARAM=`; no currents on AC results |
| Periodic steady-state (PSS / shooting / harmonic balance) | ❌ | relevant for switching converters, RF |
| S-parameter / two-port extraction | ❌ | |
| Stability / loop-gain (middlebrook, Tian) | ❌ | |

#### Device models

- **Op-amp macromodel: single pole.** `OpAmpModel` gives open-loop gain, a dominant pole from GBW, slew rate, output resistance, input offset and bias current, and a rail clamp. There is no second pole or phase margin, no output current limit, no supply current, no input common-mode range, no noise and no CMRR/PSRR. Vendor op-amp models can't be loaded. Without a `model` the op-amp is a gain-1e5 VCVS with no rail clamp.
- **Batteries are an equivalent circuit, with no chemistry.** `Battery` has an open-circuit voltage curve, a series resistance and one RC pair. Capacity doesn't fall at high current (Peukert) or in the cold, resistance doesn't rise as the cell empties, and there's no aging, self-discharge, charging limit or hysteresis between charge and discharge curves. A battery is noiseless in `.noise`, and SPICE export refuses it.
- **Regulators are linear and piecewise.** `VoltageRegulator` has dropout, quiescent current, a current limit and line and load regulation, but no foldback, thermal shutdown, PSRR that falls with frequency, or start-up behaviour. No references, adjustable regulators (LM317 with its divider) or DC-DC controllers.
- **MOSFET is Level 1 only.** No BSIM (3 / 4 / 6 / -CMG), no EKV, no PSP. Short-channel effects, velocity saturation, mobility degradation and gate leakage are absent.
- **MOSFETs have three terminals, with the body tied to the source** (as in a discrete part), so the body effect (`gamma`, `phi`) never applies in a circuit. There's no fourth body terminal for IC-style biasing to a rail.
- **BJT is Ebers-Moll with optional Early voltage.** No Gummel-Poon, no VBIC, no HICUM. No high-injection, base-width modulation in saturation, charge-storage beyond the optional Cbe/Cbc parasitic caps.
- **No JFET parasitic capacitances.** (BJT and MOSFET have optional Cbe/Cbc and Cgs/Cgd; JFET doesn't.)
- **A MOSFET's body diode is DC and junction charge only.** `body_diode` takes a full diode card (IS, N, RS, CJO, TT, BV), solved as a diode `<id>.body`; there's no separate reverse-recovery model beyond TT, and no body diode on IGBTs.
- **No SiC / GaN device models.**
- **Magnetics: a saturating inductor, no more.** `Inductor` can saturate along a smooth single-valued curve (`InductorSaturation`), but there's no hysteresis, remanence, core loss or temperature dependence, and SPICE export refuses a saturating inductor. `Transformer` is linear coupled inductors: no shared saturating core.
- **No transmission lines** (lossless or lossy / W-element).
- **No crystal / quartz resonator macromodel** (must be built from L/C/R by hand).
- **No piezo / MEMS / electro-mechanical coupling.**
- **No batteries with state-of-charge / equivalent-circuit aging.** Only ideal voltage/current sources.
- **No switched-capacitor primitives** (sample-and-hold, charge-redistribution).

#### Solver & numerics

- **Fixed-order integrators only:** Gear-2 (the default), trapezoidal and backward Euler, chosen with `TransientConfig::with_method`. No variable-order Gear. Gear-2 damps lightly-damped LC tanks slightly over many periods; trapezoidal keeps their amplitude but can ring on time constants much shorter than the step; backward Euler damps strongly.
- **Sparse LU above 100 unknowns** (`faer`), dense below. A 10 000-node resistor ladder solves in about 4 ms and a 100×100 RC mesh in about 15 ms per solve. No KLU-style partial refactorisation.
- **Convergence aids: gmin stepping, then source stepping.** When plain Newton–Raphson fails on a nonlinear DC solve, sindr retries with a gmin-stepping homotopy (`1e-2` S down to the `1e-12` floor), then by ramping every source up from zero, warm-starting between steps. `SimulationResult::convergence_aid` says which one was needed. No pseudo-transient continuation. `ConvergenceFailed` carries the iteration count and the last Newton step (not a KCL residual) to help diagnose.
- **`.nodeset`** seeds the DC operating point (`solve_circuit_with_initial_voltages`) and the bias point of AC, `.tf` and `.sens` (`solve_ac_with_initial_voltages`, `solve_tf_with_initial_voltages`, `solve_sensitivity_with_initial_voltages`).
- **A transient starts switched on at t = 0 unless asked otherwise:** `TransientConfig::new` starts from the initial conditions alone (SPICE's `UIC`), where SPICE starts from the DC operating point. `TransientStart::OperatingPoint` does what SPICE does, and a deck's `.tran` maps onto it (`uic` onto the other). The operating point it starts from is solved without self-heating. Initial winding currents on a transformer can't be set, and inductor `IC=` on SPICE element lines isn't parsed. With `tstart`, sindr's first snapshot is at `tstart` itself, where ngspice's is its first step past it.
- **Truncation-error control is per node voltage** (SPICE-style RELTOL 1e-3, VNTOL 1 µV, TRTOL 7), not per charge or flux, and the tolerances can't be changed yet. The step never exceeds `tstep`, so a coarse `tstep` buys speed only between edges.
- **No checkpointing / restart** of long transient runs.
- **No multithreading** in the solver.
- **No automatic differentiation.** Adjoint sensitivity exists for DC only, over the parameters in the table above.
- **No interval / affine arithmetic** for guaranteed bounds.

#### Self-heating & thermal

- **Self-heating is one thermal RC per part.** A part with `Part::thermal` runs at `ambient + P·Rθ` (iterated to a balance in DC, a thermal RC state in transient). There's no thermal coupling between parts (a shared heatsink, neighbours on a board), and no multi-pole Foster/Cauer ladder for the junction-to-case path.
- **Only junction devices and the thermistor feel their temperature:** diodes, LEDs, Zeners, Schottkys, photodiodes, BJTs and thermistors. MOSFETs, JFETs, IGBTs and resistors report a junction temperature (and so get Tj-max checks), but their models have no temperature in them, so heating doesn't move their operating point. Power-MOSFET and IGBT runaway is not predicted.
- **An LED's temperature coefficient is one typical figure:** Vf falls 2 mV/K at its rated 20 mA for every colour, from an effective EG per colour. Real parts range from about −1.5 to −4 mV/K.
- **Self-heating applies to `solve_circuit`, `solve_circuit_with_initial_voltages` and `solve_transient`** (and `temperature_sweep`, which sets the ambient). AC, `.tf`, `.sens` and `dc_sweep` linearise around the unheated operating point.
- In a transient the electrical step solves at the temperature from the step before. Thermal time constants are far longer than the electrical steps, so the lag doesn't matter unless the step is coarse compared with Rθ·Cθ.

#### Tooling & UX

- **No CLI**. sindr is a library only.
- **No schematic input**. Circuits are written as Rust `Vec<CircuitElement>` (or JSON via serde).
- **No KiCad / Eagle / Altium netlist import.**
- **Waveform export is CSV only.** Transient, AC and sweep results have `to_csv()`; there's no VCD, Touchstone or Common Simulation Data Format.
- **No built-in plotting**. Examples like `bode_plot.rs` produce data; rendering is on the user.
- **No interactive REPL or notebook integration.**
- **No web / WASM target tested.** It may build, but it is not a supported configuration.
- **No `no_std` support.** `nalgebra` and `std::collections::HashMap` are pulled in.

### Numerical caveats worth knowing

- Transformer coupling `k = 1.0` is mathematically singular — clamp to `≤ 0.999`.
- Switches are modelled as `0.01 Ω` / `1 GΩ` resistors — they are not ideal, and very high-impedance circuits may need explicit values.
- An op-amp without a `model`, and every comparator, is a VCVS with gain `1e5` and no frequency response or rail clamp, so its closed-loop bandwidth isn't realistic. Give the op-amp an `OpAmpModel` for GBW and slew rate. Its stage starts from 0 V at t = 0, like the capacitors, so a transient opens with a short settle unless you seed it.
- For accurate ringing amplitude in a resonant circuit, use `IntegrationMethod::Trapezoidal` with a step well below the period: Gear-2 and especially backward Euler damp it.
- Photodiode / photoresistor / thermistor "stimulus" parameters (irradiance, light level, temperature) are **constants per solve**, not time-varying inputs. There is no environmental waveform.

### Useful workarounds

- Need a vendor BJT / MOSFET? Fit Ebers-Moll / Level-1 parameters from the datasheet. Accuracy will be modest.
- Need digital control around an analog plant? Drive the analog circuit step-by-step from your own Rust loop, sampling node voltages between transient calls and updating sources / switches between them. This is not co-simulation, but it works for slow control loops.
- Need a second pole or phase margin on an op-amp? Build it from VCVS stages and RC networks around an `OpAmp` with an `OpAmpModel`.
- Need Monte Carlo? Loop in Rust over randomised `CircuitElement` parameter values; sindr is fast enough for thousands of solves on small circuits.

### Reporting gaps

If a missing capability is blocking real work, open an issue describing the **circuit and analysis you want to run**, not just the feature name — concrete use cases drive prioritisation.


# Public API of `sindr`

## `sindr/src/ac_analysis.rs`

AC small-signal analysis module.

Performs frequency-domain analysis by:
1. Finding the DC operating point (capacitors open, inductors shorted)
2. Linearizing all nonlinear elements at that point
3. Building a complex-valued MNA system at each frequency
4. Solving for node voltages as complex phasors

```rust
/// Frequency sweep spacing.
pub enum FrequencySpacing {
    /// Logarithmic spacing: `num_points` in total, evenly spaced in
    /// log10(f) from `f_start` to `f_stop`. Not points per decade.
    Logarithmic,
    /// Linear spacing.
    Linear,
}

/// AC analysis configuration.
pub struct AcConfig {
    /// Start frequency (Hz).
    pub f_start: f64,
    /// Stop frequency (Hz).
    pub f_stop: f64,
    /// Number of frequency points, including both endpoints. With 1, only
    /// `f_start` is solved.
    pub num_points: usize,
    /// Frequency spacing.
    pub spacing: FrequencySpacing,
    /// ID of the AC source (voltage source with AC stimulus).
    pub source_id: String,
    /// AC amplitude of the source: volts, linear (not dB), at 0° phase.
    /// Results scale with it; 1 V makes node voltages read as gain.
    pub ac_magnitude: f64,
}

/// Result at a single frequency point.
pub struct AcPoint {
    /// Frequency of this point (Hz).
    pub frequency: f64,
    /// Complex node voltages (V) keyed by node name. Includes the ground
    /// node (always 0).
    pub node_voltages: HashMap<String, Complex64>,
}

impl AcPoint {
    /// Gain in dB for a node: `20·log10(|V(node)| / source_magnitude)`, a
    /// voltage ratio. `source_magnitude` is in volts, normally
    /// [`AcConfig::ac_magnitude`]. `None` when the node isn't in the
    /// circuit.
    pub fn gain_db(&self, node: &str, source_magnitude: f64) -> Option<f64> { … }

    /// Phase of a node's voltage in degrees, in (−180°, 180°], relative to
    /// the source (which is at 0°). `None` when the node isn't in the
    /// circuit.
    pub fn phase_deg(&self, node: &str) -> Option<f64> { … }
}

/// Complete AC analysis result.
pub struct AcResult {
    /// Result points, one per swept frequency.
    pub points: Vec<AcPoint>,
    /// Configuration used to produce this result.
    pub config: AcConfig,
}

impl AcResult {
    /// The gain curve for a node as `(frequency in Hz, gain in dB)` pairs,
    /// one per point, using [`AcConfig::ac_magnitude`].
    pub fn gain_curve(&self, node: &str) -> Vec<(f64, f64)> { … }

    /// The phase curve for a node as `(frequency in Hz, phase in degrees)`
    /// pairs, one per point; see [`AcPoint::phase_deg`].
    pub fn phase_curve(&self, node: &str) -> Vec<(f64, f64)> { … }
}

/// Performs AC small-signal frequency-domain analysis.
///
/// Returns the complex node voltages at every frequency in the configured
/// sweep, plus helpers on [`AcResult`] for extracting gain (dB) and phase
/// (degrees) curves — i.e. Bode plot data.
///
/// # Algorithm
///
/// 1. Solve the DC operating point of `circuit`, with capacitors and
///    varactors open and inductors and transformer windings shorted.
/// 2. Linearise every nonlinear element at that operating point: diodes,
///    LEDs, Zener, Schottky and photodiodes, BJTs (full terminal Jacobian,
///    junction temperature included), MOSFETs, JFETs, IGBTs, and varactors
///    (their capacitance at the bias). A relay's contact is open or closed
///    as the bias point leaves it.
/// 3. At each frequency, build a complex-valued MNA system (capacitors and
///    inductors become `jωC` / `jωL` admittances, a transformer the coupled
///    pair `V = jω·[[L1, M], [M, L2]]·I`), solve it, and store the complex
///    node voltage phasors.
///
/// # Errors
///
/// - [`SimError::InvalidComponent`] if `config` is invalid: zero points,
///   non-finite values, `f_start > f_stop`, `f_start <= 0` with logarithmic
///   spacing, `f_start < 0` with linear spacing, or more than 10⁷ points;
///   or if `source_id` isn't the id of a voltage source in `circuit`
/// - Any [`SimError`] from the DC operating-point solve
/// - [`SimError::SingularMatrix`] if the linearised AC system is singular
///   at any frequency
///
/// # Example
///
/// ```
/// use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement};
/// use sindr::ac_analysis::{solve_ac, AcConfig, FrequencySpacing};
///
/// // Simple RC low-pass: V1 -> R1 -> n_out -> C1 -> gnd
/// let circuit = Circuit {
///     ground_node: "0".into(),
///     components: vec![
///         CircuitElement::VoltageSource {
///             id: "V1".into(),
///             nodes: ["n_in".into(), "0".into()],
///             voltage: 0.0,
///             waveform: None,
///         },
///         CircuitElement::Resistor {
///             id: "R1".into(),
///             nodes: ["n_in".into(), "n_out".into()],
///             resistance: 1_000.0,
///         },
///         CircuitElement::Capacitor {
///             id: "C1".into(),
///             nodes: ["n_out".into(), "0".into()],
///             capacitance: 1e-6,
///         },
///     ],
///     ..Default::default()
/// };
///
/// let config = AcConfig {
///     f_start: 1.0,
///     f_stop: 100_000.0,
///     num_points: 11,
///     spacing: FrequencySpacing::Logarithmic,
///     source_id: "V1".into(),
///     ac_magnitude: 1.0,
/// };
///
/// let result = solve_ac(&circuit, &config).unwrap();
/// assert_eq!(result.points.len(), 11);
///
/// // Bode plot data for the output node:
/// let gain = result.gain_curve("n_out");
/// let phase = result.phase_curve("n_out");
/// ```
pub fn solve_ac(circuit: &Circuit, config: &AcConfig) -> Result<AcResult, SimError> { … }

/// Like [`solve_ac`], seeding the Newton–Raphson solve for the DC bias
/// point with node voltages (V) keyed by node name, as SPICE's `.nodeset`.
/// Useful when the bias point is hard to find or not unique. Unknown node
/// names are ignored.
///
/// # Errors
///
/// As [`solve_ac`].
pub fn solve_ac_with_initial_voltages(
    circuit: &Circuit,
    config: &AcConfig,
    initial_voltages: &HashMap<String, f64>,
) -> Result<AcResult, SimError> { … }
```

## `sindr/src/csv.rs`

CSV export of transient, AC and sweep results.

Each result type gets a `to_csv` method that writes one row per point:
the scale (time, frequency, swept value or temperature) first, then a
column per node voltage, `v(<node>)` with nodes in name order, then
for real-valued results a column per component current, `i(<id>)`, in
circuit order. AC writes each node voltage as two columns,
`re(v(<node>))` and `im(v(<node>))`.

Numbers are written so they read back as the same `f64`. A value missing
from a row is an empty field. Names that need it are quoted as RFC 4180
has it. Lines end in `\n`.

```rust
impl TransientData {
    /// The waveforms as CSV: `time` (s), then `v(<node>)` (V) and
    /// `i(<id>)` (A, each component's `current_through`), one row per
    /// timestep. See the [module docs](crate::csv) for the layout.
    pub fn to_csv(&self) -> String { … }
}

impl DcSweepResult {
    /// The sweep as CSV: the swept source's value, in a column named after
    /// it, then `v(<node>)` (V) and `i(<id>)` (A), one row per point.
    pub fn to_csv(&self) -> String { … }
}

impl TempSweepResult {
    /// The sweep as CSV: `temperature` (K), then `v(<node>)` (V) and
    /// `i(<id>)` (A), one row per point.
    pub fn to_csv(&self) -> String { … }
}

impl AcResult {
    /// The frequency response as CSV: `frequency` (Hz), then for each node
    /// `re(v(<node>))` and `im(v(<node>))` (V, for the source's
    /// [`ac_magnitude`](crate::ac_analysis::AcConfig::ac_magnitude)), one
    /// row per frequency. Magnitude and phase follow from the two parts.
    pub fn to_csv(&self) -> String { … }
}
```

## `sindr/src/dc_sweep.rs`

DC parameter sweep module.

Sweeps a voltage or current source across a range and collects operating
point results at each step ([`dc_sweep`]), or two sources, one inside the
other ([`dc_sweep_nested`]). Used for generating I-V curves, families of
device curves and transfer characteristics.

```rust
/// One operating point of a DC sweep: the sweep value and the full result
/// at that value.
pub struct DcSweepPoint {
    /// The value of the swept source at this point (V, or A for a current
    /// source).
    pub sweep_value: f64,
    /// Full simulation result at this sweep value.
    pub result: SimulationResult,
}

/// Result of a DC sweep — one [`DcSweepPoint`] per swept value.
///
/// Use [`DcSweepResult::node_voltage_curve`] or
/// [`DcSweepResult::component_current_curve`] to extract a plottable curve.
pub struct DcSweepResult {
    /// Component id of the source that was swept.
    pub source_id: String,
    /// Operating points, in sweep order from `start` to `stop`.
    pub points: Vec<DcSweepPoint>,
}

impl DcSweepResult {
    /// `(sweep value in V, node voltage in V)` pairs for a node, one per
    /// point.
    pub fn node_voltage_curve(&self, node: &str) -> Vec<(f64, f64)> { … }

    /// `(sweep value in V, current in A)` pairs for a component, one per
    /// point. The current is its [`ComponentResult::current_through`]: from
    /// `nodes[0]` to `nodes[1]` for a two-terminal part (the collector or
    /// drain current for a transistor).
    ///
    /// [`ComponentResult::current_through`]: crate::ComponentResult::current_through
    pub fn component_current_curve(&self, component_id: &str) -> Vec<(f64, f64)> { … }
}

/// One axis of a DC sweep: a source and the values it takes, `num_points`
/// of them evenly spaced from `start` to `stop`, both included.
///
/// ```
/// use sindr::dc_sweep::DcSweepAxis;
///
/// // SPICE's `V1 0 1 0.1`: 0, 0.1, …, 1 V, eleven points.
/// let axis = DcSweepAxis::from_step("V1", 0.0, 1.0, 0.1).unwrap();
/// assert_eq!(axis.num_points, 11);
/// assert_eq!(axis.stop, 1.0);
/// ```
pub struct DcSweepAxis {
    /// Id of the [`VoltageSource`](CircuitElement::VoltageSource) or
    /// [`CurrentSource`](CircuitElement::CurrentSource) to sweep.
    pub source_id: String,
    /// First value (V or A).
    pub start: f64,
